The Lindelöf Hypothesis states that |ζ (1/2 + it)| ≪ tϵ for any ϵ > 0. If σ is real, then µ (σ ) is
defined to be the infimum of all real numbers α such that |ζ (σ + it)| = O (tα ). One has µ (σ ) = 0
for σ > 1, and the functional equation implies that µ (σ ) = µ (1 − σ ) − σ + 1/2. The Phragmén-
Lindelöf theorem implies that µ is a convex function. The Lindelöf hypothesis states µ (1/2) = 0,
which together with the above properties of µ implies that µ (σ ) is 0 for σ ≥ 1/2 and 1/2 − σ
for σ ≤ 1/2. While weaker than RH, it would still have significant applications to moments of
L-functions and subconvexity problems.

directed.source_grounded_mathematics: The conjectured 2k-th zeta moment has leading constant c_k=a_k f_k: f_k is obtained from moments of |det(I-U)| for random unitary U, while a_k is an explicit Euler product. directed.conceptual_reading: Factorization identifies a transferable universality class and a residual arithmetic correction, allowing matrix models to predict the former without pretending to encode all prime data.
directed.representation_or_bridge: Characteristic-polynomial moments supply f_k, and prime-local Euler factors supply a_k; their product is the bridge back to zeta moments.
directed.boundary_or_failure: For higher moments the asymptotics and constants remain conjectural, so random-matrix agreement is a prediction mechanism rather than a proof or exact spectral model.
